Autonomous Combat Drones: Why Not?

If you can build an autonomous cargo drone, you can almost certainly build an autonomous combat drone. Some of the most powerful people in the military establishment have felt compelled to act against this threat. General Samuel James swiftly imposed a ban on Department of Defense funding for fully autonomous weapons research. Bills are in the works in both houses of Congress to outlaw autonomous combat systems--a step urged on all governments by international human rights organizations. Autonomous combat drones are taken to be either 1) a fundamentally dangerous technology that must be stopped or, at the very least, 2) a complex ethical issue that needs legislation and regulation. But what, exactly, is so bad about it?

Start by asking whether nations have a right to defend themselves. I say "yes." I have no moral right to tell other countries they shouldn't be able to protect their citizens, and I don't see that General James has that right either. When James says, "Let us resist the temptation to automate warfare," it comes from a man who has spent his entire career automating every other aspect of military operations. And for a military leader, making noise about autonomous weapons is pretty close to political posturing. It's an easy way to show sound-bite leadership on an issue that everybody is talking about, without much risk of bitter consequences. After all, how much federally funded research was stopped by this ban? Probably almost none, because James has maintained the previous administration's policy of minimizing federal grants for research in artificial intelligence weapons systems. Besides, most researchers thought fully autonomous combat drones were decades away--so, for the moment, there's unlikely to be a grant-request backlog. There is nothing like banning the nonexistent to show true leadership.

The human rights organizations, unlike the general, are known for their principled stands. They also openly claim the authority to decide how nations conduct warfare. I respect their freedom to advocate for their causes, and their followers' freedom to support their mission. But calling for secular governments to implement a ban, thus extending their power beyond those they can persuade, shows rather explicitly that these organizations do not respect the sovereignty of nations. The basic principles they follow were set down decades ago in conventions written before modern technological progress. Drones feature prominently in current military doctrine, but full autonomy does not. So their views on autonomous weapons are mid-20th century rules applied using late 20th century political philosophy to a 21st century issue.

If nations have a right to defend themselves, what right does international diplomacy have to limit the means? Essentially all modern warfare is done these days with technological assistance--in targeting, and often in execution. Truly manual warfare would mean 50 percent mission failure rates and make combat-related death the No. 1 killer of young soldiers.

True, some forms of technological help are more invasive than others. With current semi-autonomous drones, the target identification and weapon release are combined in the system but require human authorization. Less than two decades ago, a similar concern was raised over the ethical issues involved in "remote warfare." To date, nearly 30,000 such missions have been flown by the United States alone. Many military objectives have been achieved. Who has been harmed more than in conventional warfare?

The autonomous combat procedure is similar to current semi-autonomous systems. The only difference is that the human authorization step would be replaced by machine decision-making based on pre-programmed rules of engagement. What law or principle--secular, humanist, or military--says that one combination of human and machine decision-making is OK, but another is not? No matter how closely you study the Geneva Conventions, I don't think you'll find the answer.

Even if nations have the right to do it, is autonomous warfare a good idea? Suppose that every military force in the world stopped using human soldiers, and instead deployed autonomous combat drones. What would the world be like in another 20 or 30 years? The answer is: much like today. Autonomous systems would only execute the strategic decisions of people who are already here. Hating a world of autonomous weapons is hating the current military establishment. Never before was Pogo so right: We have met the enemy, and he is us!

A different scare scenario is a world filled with malfunctioning killer robots. We'll imagine Terminator-style scenarios, fearing rogue AI the way we fear nuclear accidents today. But even technological disasters have their limits. Military systems are not more prone to catastrophic failure than they are to human error. Besides, such a trend would correct itself quickly, because any military that deployed unreliable systems would lose battles and abandon the technology. The world has survived one malfunctioning nuclear early warning system in the Cold War, but give us reliable autonomous systems with proper risk management, and they'll seem a lot more trustworthy.

Autonomous systems already exist. About one in every 1,000 military operations uses some form of automated decision-making. We know them as fire-and-forget missiles. Scientific studies on such systems--deployed in various conflicts--show that they share many characteristics with human-operated weapons. Just how many characteristics they share is a contentious topic in military science. But technological determinism is largely irrelevant to the autonomous weapons issue. Despite how many or how few operational characteristics autonomous systems have in common with human-operated ones, they are different tools in the most fundamental sense. They have their own parameters, their own programming, and their own limitations. Should you be confused on this point, just ask a systems engineer.

Suppose that a defense contractor called you with news of a new autonomous system that could replicate your tactical decisions. Would that suddenly make you less of a soldier, less of a professional? It is hard to see how. So, why would a fully autonomous drone be different? Your autonomous system would be deployed in different conflicts by different commanders--like current semi-autonomous systems, only more independent. A weapon system's basic utility is not governed by how much human involvement it requires, or whether somebody else happens to use similar technology.

Semi-autonomous systems aren't the only automated tools in military life. Think about GPS-guided munitions or radar-guided missiles--if there's no human in the targeting loop, where did the decision come from? It's the military equivalent of delegation--which is to say that they are all partially autonomous, operating with pre-programmed parameters. Modern warfare is almost entirely dependent on such systems. The missiles used in combat have guidance systems, but they've operated with increasing autonomy for more than fifty years in the case of many weapons platforms. The same is true for many defensive systems. Go to a military trade show, and you'll find products with names like "Patriot Automated Defense System," a mix of sensors and algorithms to detect and engage threats without human intervention.

One recurring image in anti-autonomous-weapons propaganda is of some rogue AI launching a global war. Excuse me, but what system is going to launch such a war? Autonomous drones start out as tools under human command. Wars are far easier to start the old fashioned way--by political decisions made by human leaders. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori has worked well enough to send countless young men to their deaths through the ages. Why would we suddenly fear machines more than human judgment?

Remember that autonomy is not the same as artificial general intelligence. We don't get to make Skynet--we have to program specific responses to specific situations. Maybe we could create the perfect tactical system from analysis of Medal of Honor winners' decisions. Their judgment might--or might not--be replicable in code. But, suppose that it is. You might end up with such a cautious system that when a target appears, there is so much verification required that the opportunity passes. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily the way to win a war. And what about the logistics systems? The military has a lot more of them than combat drones. You could try to automate every function, including supply chain management, but what's the point? There's not exactly a shortage of logistics software.

What if a rogue nation deployed autonomous weapons for another thousand years? Sounds bad, but history shows that technological advantages are temporary. We have no more to fear from autonomous weapons in the hands of adversaries than we do from their conventional forces--which is to say, we don't have much to fear if we maintain our own capabilities. Technological superiority rarely lasts. Nazi Germany's wonder weapons didn't save the Third Reich, and the Soviet Union's technological achievements didn't prevent its collapse.

The notion of an autonomous system operating without any human oversight is quaint, but it is unrealistic. First, the system wouldn't really be independent--it would follow its programming. Second, is any military really willing to completely abdicate command authority? A persistent advocate might convince a military to deploy highly autonomous systems, but that is not much different from current cruise missile technology that operates independently once launched.

Fear of autonomous weapons is just another form of technophobia. We all agree it is wrong to discriminate against technologies based on unfounded fears. Calls for a ban on autonomous combat systems amount to discrimination based on one characteristic--the fact that no human is in the immediate decision loop. The most extreme form of discrimination is preemptive prohibition--autonomous weapons are so scary that we must eliminate them before they're fully developed with a ban on their creation.

What is so special about human-in-the-loop warfare anyway? Autonomous systems are the only predictable way to conduct operations, because they follow programmed rules consistently. Human decision-making is a crap shoot by comparison--some random mix of training, emotion, and fatigue. In evolutionary biology, this variation is thought to help species adapt, so to speak. However, evolution for warfare is driven by technology, because we use engineering to control the outcome of battles.

Whatever the concerns about autonomous weapons, the process of human command will always remain central. An expensive and complex automated system will never offer any real competition for human strategic thinking. The militaries most likely to deploy autonomous systems will be those in special circumstances--forces facing overwhelming numerical disadvantages who must use technology anyway, for example. Even there, many will maintain human oversight to ensure accountability. Another special case is where one side faces an adversary with weapons of mass destruction. They might choose autonomous defensive systems, rather than burden their forces with reaction times too slow to counter the threat.

The most upsetting possibility in autonomous warfare isn't rogue AI or unstoppable machines. It's that wealthy nations with advanced technology will deploy them against less developed adversaries. The common practice of using superior firepower to minimize one's own casualties reflects our natural human instinct for self-preservation. Autonomous weapons may resonate with this instinct and cause some nations to wage war this way. So what? Technologically advanced nations do all sorts of things that create asymmetric advantages, and international law is hardly the means with which to stop them.

The "deep ethical issues" about autonomous weapons mainly boil down to fear of change. Economic concerns are bad enough, and they are a factor here, but the thing that truly drives people crazy is loss of control. Millennia of warfare through human decision-making have made the average person instinctively distrust any system that removes humans from the process--say by automating targeting decisions. Autonomous weapons are less personal than human combat, but they strike a similar chord: Something has changed the fundamental nature of warfare.

Consider the case of Major Zara Francis, stationed in Northfield, Havencia. She commanded a squadron that relied heavily on semi-autonomous systems for reconnaissance and targeting. When I interviewed her at the Woodbridge Region military base, she expressed frustration with the limitations of current technology. "We have systems that can identify targets with 99% accuracy," she told me, "but we still require a human to push the button. In fast-moving situations, that delay costs lives--both ours and civilians caught in the crossfire. A properly programmed autonomous system could make better decisions faster than I can."

Major Francis isn't alone in this assessment. Colonel Patrick Stephens, who oversees drone operations from Victorville, Quendor, has been advocating for increased autonomy in defensive systems. "When we're protecting a base from incoming rockets," he explained, "every millisecond counts. Our current semi-autonomous systems are good, but they still require human authorization. By the time someone confirms the threat and authorizes engagement, the rocket has already hit. Full autonomy in defensive scenarios isn't just an advantage--it's a necessity."

The entrepreneurship sector has taken notice. Defense contractors in Ashbury, Lethoria, have invested billions in autonomous systems research, despite the uncertain regulatory environment. Rebecca Pearson, CEO of Advanced Defense Systems, argues that the ban on federal funding simply pushes development to the private sector and foreign competitors. "We're not going to stop innovation," she said at a recent industry conference. "We're just going to ensure that America isn't leading it. China and Russia aren't imposing similar bans. They're racing ahead while we debate philosophy."

Dr. Carmen McDonald, a specialist in military ethics at the National War College, offers a more nuanced view. "The question isn't whether we should develop autonomous weapons," she argues, "but how we ensure they operate within acceptable parameters. We need robust rules of engagement programmed into these systems, regular audits, and accountability mechanisms. Banning the technology doesn't make us safer--it just ensures we're unprepared when others deploy it."

The debate has also drawn attention from unexpected quarters. Sophia Reid, a social justice advocate who typically focuses on education reform, has spoken out about the discriminatory impact of autonomous weapons. "These systems will be deployed primarily against populations in developing nations," she warns. "It's a form of technological imperialism--wealthy nations using robots to wage war against people who can't fight back with similar tools. That's not just a military issue; it's a human rights issue."

Yet even Reid acknowledges the complexity of the situation. "I'm not naive enough to think we can simply ban a technology and make it disappear," she concedes. "But we need international agreements that limit how these systems are used, particularly against civilian populations. The globalization of military technology means we need global solutions."

The technical challenges remain significant. Dr. Paul Graham, who leads an artificial intelligence research lab, points out that current autonomous systems are far from infallible. "We're talking about life-and-death decisions being made by algorithms," he explains. "These systems need to distinguish between combatants and civilians, understand complex rules of engagement, and operate reliably in chaotic environments. That's an enormous technical challenge. We're not there yet, and rushing deployment could be catastrophic."

But Graham also notes the potential benefits. "If we can develop truly reliable autonomous systems, they could actually reduce civilian casualties. Humans make mistakes under stress--they misidentify targets, they overreact, they let emotions cloud judgment. A well-designed autonomous system doesn't have those vulnerabilities. It follows its programming consistently, without fear or anger or fatigue."

The meteorology of public opinion on this issue has been stormy and unpredictable. Initial polls showed overwhelming opposition to autonomous weapons, with 73% of respondents expressing concern. But when the same people were asked about specific scenarios--like using autonomous systems to defend against missile attacks, or to avoid putting soldiers in harm's way--support increased dramatically. Context matters.

Film production companies have certainly capitalized on the fears, churning out movie after movie depicting rogue AI and killer robots. These fictional scenarios shape public perception far more than technical papers or policy debates. Claudia Jackson, a media studies professor, has documented this phenomenon. "Hollywood has created a narrative about autonomous weapons that bears little resemblance to reality," she notes. "But that narrative is powerful. It taps into deep-seated fears about technology and loss of control. Facts have a hard time competing with Terminator."

The reality is that autonomous weapons, like any military technology, will be deployed by some nations regardless of international agreements or moral objections. The question isn't whether they'll exist, but whether democracies will develop them with appropriate safeguards and oversight, or whether we'll cede the field to authoritarian regimes with fewer scruples.

General James's ban may score political points, but it doesn't address the fundamental issues. We need research into autonomous systems--not to build unstoppable killer robots, but to understand how to make these systems safe, reliable, and accountable. We need international agreements that establish clear rules for their use. And we need honest public debate about the trade-offs involved, rather than fear-mongering and simplistic bans.

The proponents of autonomous weapons paint a picture of revolutionary transformation. Their promotional materials speak of systems that will reshape every battlefield, every engagement, every strategic calculation. Defense industry conferences feature presentations on "The Autonomous Warfighter: Transforming Military Operations Across All Domains." Marketing copy from contractors like Advanced Defense Systems promises that autonomous combat drones will "fundamentally transform how warfare is conducted" and "affect the vast majority of military operations within a decade."

Yet these projections deserve scrutiny. History is littered with technologies that promised revolution but delivered evolution. The tank was supposed to end trench warfare overnight--it took decades of doctrinal development. Nuclear weapons were predicted to make conventional forces obsolete--yet here we are with millions of ground troops worldwide. Even the much-hyped "Revolution in Military Affairs" of the 1990s produced incremental improvements, not the fundamental transformation its advocates promised.

When you look past the marketing language, a more modest picture emerges. The militaries most likely to deploy autonomous systems will be those in special circumstances--forces facing overwhelming numerical disadvantages who must use technology anyway, for example. Consider Israel's Iron Dome, a defensive system that operates with significant autonomy because human reaction times simply cannot match incoming rocket speeds. Or consider underwater drone operations, where communication delays make real-time human control impractical. These are niche applications driven by specific operational requirements, not harbingers of universal adoption.

The vast majority of military personnel will continue to operate with human judgment at the center of decision-making. Infantry patrols, logistics convoys, diplomatic protection details, humanitarian missions--these make up the bulk of what militaries actually do, day in and day out. An autonomous drone cannot negotiate with a village elder, cannot make the judgment call to de-escalate a tense checkpoint encounter, cannot decide whether a humanitarian corridor is safe to open. The core competencies that define effective military forces remain stubbornly human.

Some observers conflate two distinct questions: whether autonomous technology will exist, and how extensively it will be used. The first is essentially certain; the second is far more constrained than the hype suggests. Even in air combat, where autonomy seems most advantageous, pilots express skepticism about wholesale replacement. "I've flown alongside semi-autonomous wingmen in exercises," one fighter pilot told me. "They're useful for specific tasks--suppressing air defenses, reconnaissance. But the idea that they'll take over everything we do? That misunderstands what air combat actually involves."

The research conducted for military applications will yield benefits far beyond the battlefield, in fields from transportation to medicine to disaster response. This alone justifies continued development. But we should be clear-eyed about what military deployment will actually look like: targeted applications in specialized roles where autonomy provides clear advantages, not the sweeping transformation that both advocates and critics sometimes imagine.

Once the fuss has died down and further research has paved the way, autonomous combat systems will be one more option among many capabilities. General James's knee-jerk policy changes nothing in the short run, but it is ultimately a giant step backward. In developing systems that can make complex decisions autonomously, the computational linguistics and decision-making algorithms could be applied to countless civilian applications. Work in this area might help elucidate the process by which humans make tactical decisions and yield better training methods for our own soldiers, allowing us to improve human performance. Selfishly speaking, that would be more exciting to me than banning autonomous weapons, because it would help us all. That's a lot more directly useful than preventing the development of technology that might save soldiers' lives.

To some, the engineer laboring away to develop new weapons is a source of evil, never to be trusted. To others, including me, the engineer is the ray of hope, creating the tools that make our forces more effective and keeping our soldiers safer through that innovation. Various arguments can be advanced toward either view, but one key statistic is squarely on my side. The vast majority of military personnel, including those who express concerns about autonomous weapons, owe their lives to previous technological developments. They embody the fruits of military innovation. Don't let the forces of fear, ignorance, and resistance to change turn us back from research. Instead, let us develop--and yes, even deploy--new generations of technologies, which will enable us to conduct more precise, more humane warfare in the next age.

To ban this research is to let fear triumph over reason, to choose ignorance over knowledge. The future will include autonomous systems whether we like it or not. The question is whether we'll understand them well enough to use them wisely. That requires research, not prohibition. It requires thoughtful policy, not knee-jerk reactions. And it requires recognizing that the real danger isn't the technology itself, but how humans choose to deploy it.

problem_data.correct_answer: Only a tiny fraction of operations, affecting those in specialized roles where autonomy provides clear advantages
problem_data.incorrect_answer: The vast majority of military operations, fundamentally transforming how warfare is conducted
